sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Purpose note and imports
sections.what: Explains that this file is a fixture-based control for the numeric provenance validator. It imports the validator, the numeral matcher and the shared types.
sections.why: The header explains that a validator which only ever says untraceable would look identical to a broken measurement.
sections.watch_out: Passing here does not prove any live artifact is well traced.

sections.name: index
sections.title: Fake evidence and computation records
sections.what: Builds a small set of fake source rows, some with a matching quoted sentence, some with no quote, and one client-supplied file with no web address. It also builds two computation records, one that agrees with its number and one that does not.
sections.why: The validator takes this snapshot as an argument, so tests need no database.
sections.watch_out: The quoted sentences must contain the same numbers as the test claims, so editing one without the other breaks expectations.

sections.name: claims
sections.title: Eight fake numbers
sections.what: Lists eight numbers, each labelled with a letter and a comment that says which class or cause it should produce, such as a sourced figure, a computed figure, or a number whose quote does not contain it.
sections.why: Each case covers one class or one cause of untraceability.
sections.watch_out: The labels are only letters, so the expected results in the next section must match them exactly.

sections.name: expected
sections.title: Expected results and validator run
sections.what: Maps each letter to its expected class, runs the validator in warn mode, and prints PASS or FAIL for each number.
sections.why: Confirms every class and cause is actually reached.
sections.watch_out: Results are looked up by path letter, so two numbers using the same path would overwrite each other's expectation.

sections.name: matcherCases
sections.title: Numeral matcher and rate checks
sections.what: Tests the matcher on sample sentences, such as US$1.2 billion matching 1200 million and a spelled-out two-year delay not matching. It then checks the traceable rate is three of eight, that the report would block, and that warn mode does not enforce.
sections.why: The scale-word handling keeps billions and millions from looking like a mismatch. Spelled-out numbers are excluded on purpose.
sections.watch_out: Real documents that write numbers in words will show as untraceable, because the matcher skips them.

summary: Self-test for the E25 numeric provenance validator, which checks whether each number in an artifact can be traced to a source or a computation.
purpose: Shows that the validator can return all four classes and every untraceable cause, so its live results mean something.
why: The header says the live measurement returned 0 percent traceable everywhere, which a validator that only says untraceable would also produce. This test proves the other answers are reachable.
how: Builds a fake provenance index with evidence rows and computation records. Defines eight fake numbers, each meant to land in a specific class. Runs the validator in warn mode and compares each result to its expected class. Then checks the numeral matcher on sample sentences and checks the traceable rate and the warn-mode flags.
inputs: Only built-in fixtures. No database, model or network.
outputs: A PASS or FAIL line for each number, for each matcher case, and for the rate and mode checks. Exits 0 when all pass and 1 otherwise.
risks: Passing shows the logic works on fixtures only. It does not show that live numbers are traced correctly. The matcher does not recognise spelled-out numbers, so real text written in words will not match.
debug: Run npx tsx script/verify-e25.ts. Check the first FAIL line. If a class is wrong, look at the validator. If a matcher case fails, look at the numeral matcher and its scale-word handling.
